list.listitem: Determine the pretest probability of coronary artery disease (CAD) in all patients with typical and atypical angina. B
Stratify risk using noninvasive testing, including rest ECG for patients with typical/atypical angina B and an exercise tolerance test for patients with intermediate probability of CAD. B
Advise patients to quit smoking. B

All patients with CAD should be taking the following medications unless contraindicated: aspirin A , a high intensity statin A , and a beta-blocker A for patients with history of myocardial infarction (MI), angina, or left ventricular systolic dysfunction.
For patients with CAD and DM/left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction, add an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor A , unless contraindicated. A
Immediate-acting nitroglycerin (sublingual/spray) provides relief of anginal symptoms. B
Long-acting calcium channel blockers and Ranolazine are useful adjuncts or substitutes for symptom reduction if beta-blockers are ineffective or contraindicated. B
In most patients, optimal medical treatment may be as effective as PCIs followed by optimal medical treatment in the management of patients with stable CAD. A

background.definition: Stable angina (SA) is a clinical syndrome characterized by discomfort in the chest (or jaw, shoulder, back, or arm) that is aggravated by physical activity and/or emotional stress and relieved by rest and/or nitroglycerin. It is a common presentation of ischemic heart disease (IHD) and coronary heart disease (CHD).

list.listitem:
All the figures are based on the American Heart Association's (AHA) Heart and Stroke Statistics 2021 Update
Heart disease is the leading cuase of death in the US and accounted for approximately 13% of deaths in the US in 2018. According to data from 2005 to 2014, the estimated annual incidence of heart attack in the US was 605,000 new attacks and 200,000 recurrent attacks. Average age at first heart attack was 65.6 years for males and 72 years for females

All the figures are based on the AHA Heart and Stroke Statistics 2021 Update. Approximately every 39 seconds, an American will have a heart attack. About 659,000 people in the United States die from heart disease each year. About 18.2 million adults age 20 and older have coronary artery disease (about 6.7%).
The average annual estimated direct and indirect cost of heart disease in 2016 to 2017 was $219.6 billion
Heart attacks ($ 12.1 billion) and CHD ($9.0billion) were 2 of the 10 most expensive conditions treated in US hospitals in 2013.
Black-white disparities in mortality persist, particularly for the 35- to 64-year-old age group.
Risk factors include non-modifiable and modifiable factors (see Risk Factors).
Fatty streaks begin to accumulate on the intima of coronary arteries in late adolescence/early adulthood.
Fibrous atherosclerotic plaques narrow the lumen(s) and impede blood flow.
Increased oxygen demand or decreased oxygen supply lead to chest pain/angina.
Plaque rupture and thrombosis can abruptly narrow the lumen in acute coronary syndromes (ACS), which includes unstable angina.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Personal history of stroke or peripheral vascular disease

list.listitem: Screen for and manage modifiable CAD risk factors: blood pressure A ; blood sugar C ; lipids B ; tobacco use A ; and weight in patients with hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or diabetes. C
Discuss the benefits and risks of aspirin use in patients at increased risk for CAD. A

Multiple risk calculators are available online (in websites such as the American College of Cardiology), to estimate the 10-year risk of Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease (ASCVD). These are based on the ACC/AHA guidelines on primary prevention of cardiovascular disease

All recommendations below from the United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF).
Screen all adults older than 20 years for high blood pressure, tobacco use, and obesity. Screen for dyslipidemia in men older than 34 years and women older than 44 years; also screen men between the ages of 20 years and 35 years and women between the ages of 20 years to 45 years who have CAD risk factors. Screen for type 2 diabetes in adults with hypertension and/or hyperlipidemia; also screen in adults who are overweight/obese, fall into a high-risk group (blacks, Latinos, Pacific Islanders), or have a family history of diabetes. Do not screen low-risk adults with ECG, exercise treadmill test, or computerized tomography; evidence is insufficient to recommend routine screening of high-risk patients using these tests. Among asymptomatic patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes, use of Coronary Computerized Tomography Angiography (CCTA) to screen for CAD did not reduce the rate of all-cause mortality, nonfatal MI, or unstable angina requiring hospitalization at 4 years

Primary prevention includes control of blood pressure in all age groups (systolic blood pressure lower than 130 recommended based on the SPRINT studyand the STEP study), blood sugar, and lipids (see NCEP III); weight management; and smoking cessation.

Aspirin is no longer routinely recommended for primary prevention of ASCVD.The draft recommendation USPSTF statement (2021) concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults ages 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit. The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults age 60 years or older has no net benefit.
Vitamin E not recommended for primary prevention of CHD; it may have adverse CVD effects.
Secondary prevention includes management of modifiable risk factors with nonpharmacologic measures (diet, exercise, weight management) and pharmacologic measures.
Smoking cessation, blood pressure control lower than 130 recommended in all age groups

Medications used in secondary prevention include aspirin (75-162 mg), beta-blockers, and lipid lowering drugs; as well as ACE inhibitors, especially in those with diabetes and those with and an ejection fraction of less than 40% without severe renal disease.
Current guidelines from the American Heart Association recommend high intensity statin therapy for individuals with cardiovascular disease. See drug therapy section for a more detailed discussion.
For patients whose LDL is not at goal despite maximum tolerated statin therapy, addition of PCSK9 inhibitors Alirocumab and Evolucumab have been shown to improve cardiovascular outcomes
Patients with cardiovascular disease should have an influenza vaccine.
Determine the probability of CHD on the basis of patient age, sex, CHD risk factors, and pain characteristics. B

Among patients with stable coronary artery disease and moderate or severe ischemia, there is no evidence that an initial invasive strategy as compared to with an initial conservative strategy, reduced the risk of ischemic cardiovascular events or death. It may be therefore reasonable to treat patients with stable coronary artery disease with optimal medical therapy first prior to considering invasive testing.

Exercise ECG treadmill test is the initial test of choice for risk stratification in patients with an intermediate pretest probability who are able to exercise and have a normal resting electrocardiogram. B

Use enhanced exercise treadmill test (with echocardiography or myocardial perfusion imaging) for patients with intermediate probability of CAD and any of following: (1) Wolff-Parkinson-White, (2) >1 mm ST depression at rest, (3) prior revascularization (percutaneous coronary intervention [PCI] or CABG), (4) digoxin use, (5) inability to exercise. Paced rhythms or left bundle branch block on ECG is an indication for vasodilator myocardial perfusion imaging. B
Coronary angiography recommended as initial test for patients with known or possible angina who have survived sudden cardiac death with a reasonable expectation for recovery. B

Differential.Differential_Features: More severe than angina, >30 min duration, elevated cardiac enzymes
Sharp pain; radiates to trapezius; worsened by inspiration; relieved by sitting forward
Sudden, knifelike/tearing; anterior/posterior midscapular; asymmetric blood pressure/pulses
Sudden, pleuritic, unilateral pain; decreased breath sounds; hyperresonance; chest x-ray findings
Pleuritic, dyspnea, fever, cough, sputum, infiltrate on chest x-ray
Substernal burning; aggravated by meals, recumbency; relieved by antacids
Intense substernal pain; aggravated by swallowing; relieved by nitroglycerin or beta-blockers
Epigastric pain relieved by antacids; may be accompanied by hematemesis or melena
Right upper quadrant pain; nausea/vomiting; aggravated by fatty foods
Localized; sharp/dull pain; aggravated by positional changes; tender to palpation
Precipitated by movement; lasts seconds to hours
Intense; unilateral pain with or without rash in dermatomal distribution

list.listitem: Pain location: substernal with or without radiation to neck, jaw, epigastrium, or arms.

Pain quality: "discomfort" or "pain"; described as a pressure, heaviness, stabbing, squeezing, grip-like, or suffocating. Positive Levine sign (patient clutches chest with clenched fist) is hallmark of angina.
Pain duration: typically lasts minutes (not seconds or hours).
Modifying factors: aggravated by physical exertion or emotional stress; and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin.
Presence of risk factors (e.g., hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesteremia) or signs/stigmata associated with risk factors (e.g., retinopathy, microalbuminuria) increase the likelihood of CAD.
Signs predictive of CAD (e.g., gallops, mitral regurgitation, paradoxically split S2) may be detected during a pain episode.
Risk stratification by clinical parameters (). Patients with acute angina should be categorized as stable or unstable.
Lab tests evaluate for risk factors, including glycosylated hemoglobin, fasting glucose, and fasting lipid profile.
Resting EKG is normal in 49% of patients but should be obtained in patients without obvious non-cardiac chest pain.
Chest x-ray is often normal. Abnormalities may be found in patients with prior MI, CHF, valvular dysfunction, and pulmonary disease.

Computerized tomography characterizes coronary artery calcification (which is equivalent to coronary artery plaques); the clinical efficacy of this test for augmenting disease outcomes remains uncertain, but may have a role in informing decisions for medical therapy (i.e., statins) in asymptomatic patients.
Routine EKG or stress EKG testing is not recommended in asymptomatic low-risk patients (who are not employed in high-risk professions, i.e., airline pilots).

Exercise treadmill testing is the initial test for risk stratification for intermediate risk patients who are able to exercise, not taking digoxin, have a resting EKG that is normal or have less than 1 mm of ST depression at rest ().

Stress testing with nuclear or echocardiographic imaging studies is reserved for patients w/baseline ECG abnormalities (>1 mm ST depression at rest) or prior revascularization and is also considered an option for women (given their decreased sensitivity to the nonenhanced exercise treadmill test (see ).

Pharmacologic agents used in enhanced stress testing include adenosine, dipyridamole, and regadenason (vasodilators usually used with myocardial perfusion scintigraphy). Consider using them in patients with an intermediate probability of CAD and an electronically paced rhythm or left bundle-branch block, or those unable to exercise. Dobutamine infusion with echocardiographic imaging is another option for patients unable to exercise.

Echocardiography should be considered in patients with patients with known or suspected CAD and prior myocardial infarction, heart failure, complex ventricular arrhythmias, or an undiagnosed heart murmur.

CT coronary angiography can identify the presence and severity of obstructive CAD (stenosis of 50% or more; sensitivity of 85%, specificity of 90%) and subsequent revascularization (in symptomatic patients). The sensitivity of CT appears to be lower for women.
CT coronary angiography bears similar long term risks as invasive coronary angiography in patients with stable chest pain.

Among low-risk patients, fractional flow reserve (FFRCT) using CT angiography as compared to standard care was not different in producing better outcomes of patient symptoms, quality of life, MACE or use of coronary revascularisation. However, initial use of FFRCT lead to a significant 22% reduction in invasive coronary angiography. Whether this cost benefit can be extrapolated to other health systems in the world needs further study.
Invasive testing/coronary angiography is the gold standard and initial test for patients surviving sudden death from ventricular arrhythmias who have a reasonable expectation for functional recovery.
A number of clinical rules can help guide treatment.
Risk of left main or severe CAD can be estimated using clinical rules.
Clinical rules can also help guide interpretation of exercise treadmill test.

Perform focused history and physical and classify pain as angina or noncardiac chest pain ().
Include an ECG in initial testing if the cause of chest pain is not obviously non-cardiac.
Assess the patient’s functional limitation as a result of the chest pain using the Canadian Cardiovascular Society classification system ().
Determine the pretest probability of CHD on the basis of the patient’s age, sex, and classification of pain (e.g., typical angina).
The probability of CHD increases with age and is higher for men than women and for those with typical angina versus noncardiac chest pain ().
Stratify risk based on a clinical decision tool and appropriate use of stress testing (with or without imaging) or coronary CT angiography.
Use aspirin for primary C and secondary A preventive treatment.
Use ACE inhibitors for all patients with diabetes B , especially those with CAD A ; also patients with CAD and systolic dysfunction. A
Use beta-blockers for all patients with prior MI A ; may also be beneficial for those without prior MI. B
Use sublingual nitrates for symptomatic relief, and consider ranolazine for symptomatic relief in patients with refractory chronic angina. B
In most patients, optimal medical treatment may be as effective as PCIs followed by optimal medical treatment in the management of patients with stable CAD. A

Treatment for stable angina (SA) can be grouped into drugs that affect (1) mortality and morbidity (occurrence of MI): aspirin (or clopidogrel), beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and statins; and (2) drugs that affect symptoms only: nitrates and long-acting calcium channel blockers.

Aspirin is recommended as first-line antiplatelet agent for all patients without contraindications. Low-dose aspirin preferable given reduced gastrointestinal side effects and comparable reduction in vascular events compared with higher doses (meta-analyses of aspirin doses between 75 and 325 mg).

Use clopidogrel if aspirin is contraindicated. Aspirin plus a proton pump inhibitor is preferred to clopidogrel in patients with history of gastrointestinal bleed given higher bleeding rates associated with latter. Aspirin may be combined with clopidogrel for patients with non-ST elevation ACS or recurrent ACS.
Prolonged antiplatelet therapy may have benefit in reducing cardiovascular events, but prolonged use is associated with increased bleeding risk.

In patients who are at high risk for bleeding after implantation of a drug-eluting stent, one month of dual antiplatelet therapy is noninferior to the continuation of therapy for at least 2 additional months with regard to major adverse cardiovascular events and is also associated with a lower incidence of major or clinically relevant bleeding

Beta-blockers are recommended for all patients with prior MI and may be helpful for CAD without prior MI if angina is present; titrate dose to reduce heart rate to 55 to 60 bpm and systolic blood pressure to less than 130 mm Hg. Beta-blockers are less effective for patients with vasospastic angina without evidence of fixed plaques (ie, Prinzmetal angina); use a calcium channel blocker instead.

ACE inhibitors are recommended especially for patients with diabetes, LV systolic dysfunction, and/or known CAD or vascular disease (see HOPE trial). One RCT study found no benefit in low-risk patients with normal LV function.

Statins are recommended for patients with cardiovascular disease. Specifically, AHA guidelines recommend a high intensity statin (atorvastatin 40-80 mg or rosuvastatin 20-40 mg). A retrospective cohort study in the VA population found a graded favorable impact on all-cause mortality, with a hazard ratio of 0.91 for the comparison of high- vs moderate-intensity statins (95% CI 0.88-0.93).
For patients with CAD whose LDL is not at goal despite maximum tolerated statin therapy, addition of PCSK9 inhibitors will reduce LDL further and result in better cardiovascular outcomes
Ranolazine increases exercise capacity and provides additional antiaginal relief in symptomatic patients with severe chronic angina taking beta-blockers

Long-acting/slow-release dihydropyridine or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers or long-acting nitrates can be used as adjunct therapy or if beta-blockers are contraindicated or not tolerated.
See for a recommended treatment algorithm.
Use of folate therapy in patients with elevated homocysteine levels has been recommended, but studies have found increased risk of stent restenosis and no evidence of benefit for primary prevention.
Methotrexate therapy was found to have no benefit in prevention of secondary events in patients with coronary artery disease.

For most patients with stable coronary artery disease without obstructive left main or proximal left anterior descending coronary artery disease, there is no evidence that invasive therapy is of added survival benefit over optimal medical management.

The 2021 ACC/AHA guidelines recommend CABG for patients with stable ischemic heart disease (SIHD) and LV dysfunction (< 35%) and for selected patients with moderate dysfunction (35% to 50%). PCI or CABG are also recommended for patients with left main coronary artery disease.

The 2021 ACC/AHA guidelines note that for patients with SIHD and a normal ejection fraction and significant 3 vessel disease, CABG is an option, while PCI is of uncertain benefit in these patients. The value of revascularization is also uncertain for patients with proximal left anterior descending stenosis.

ACC/AHA guidelines (2021) also recommend radial artery over femoral artery access. Dual antiplatelet therapy is recommended following PCI for 1 to 3 months, with most patients able to discontinue aspirin at that point.
Revascularization is not recommended for patients with 1 or 2 vessel disease not involving proximal LAD who have normal ejection fraction.

In the largest RCT of intensive medical therapy versus PCI (followed by intensive medical therapy) for patients with stable CAD (N = 2287), there was no difference between groups in a composite of death or nonfatal myocardial infarction (19% in each) or in all-cause mortality (8% in each group). Patients with severe left main coronary artery stenosis were excluded from this study. A considerable portion of patients randomized to the medical therapy arm received PCI for recurrent angina.

In one small RCT of PCI versus intensive medical therapy for patients with SA, PCI was associated with modest symptomatic and quality of life benefit for the first postprocedural year (NNT = 9-11) that diminished over time to no difference at 36 months.

A study of 5179 patients with stable CAD randomized to medical therapy versus an initial invasive strategy for moderate to severe ischemia on noninvasive testing found a nonsignificant trend towards reduced MI or CV death in the invasive strategy among patients with greater number of involved vessels; otherwise there was no significant difference in the primary outcome.

A randomized trial of 1845 patients found no advantage to using bioresorbable vascular scaffold over metallic stent for patients undergoing PCI; there was a higher risk of device thrombosis (3.5% vs 0.9%, p <0.001, NNT = 20).

Even among high-risk patients, an initial trial of optimal medical therapy did not increase the rates of death or myocardial infarction at 4.6 years or more severe angina at 1 year; in the first year, 30% of patients in the medical therapy group were referred for revascularization.

CABG is primarily for significant left main or 3-vessel CAD; or 2-vessel disease with significant proximal LAD and either an ejection fraction of less than 50% or ischemia on noninvasive testing. Data suggests that CABG may preferred over PCI for patients with diabetes.

A large trial with 4752 patients found no difference in cardiovascular outcomes, renal failure, or mortality for patients undergoing off-pump vs on-pump CABG. There is also no difference in outcomes for patients receiving biilateral vs single internal thoracic artery (mammary artery) grafts, based on an RCT with 3102 patients.

listitem.strong: Other surgeries and comparisons of PCI with CABG

list.listitem: A trial randomized 1500 patients with 3 vessel coronary disease to CABG or fractional flow reserve (FFR) guided PCI with drug eluting stent. For the compositive of death, stroke, or MI, FFR guided PCI was non non-inferior (e.g. was inferior) to CABG (7.3% vs 5.2%).
Coronary sinus-reduction with an implanted device has been shown to reduce refractory angina in one study.

A small study of patients with CAD who underwent stenting versus a sham intervention found no significant difference in exercise tolerance or angina symptoms; all patients were treated with medical therapy for CAD.
Diets low in fat and high in fiber, antioxidants, and monosaturated fats or fish are highly recommended, as is increased physical activity and weight management.
There is inconclusive evidence on the potential benefits of coenzyme Q, garlic, or acupuncture.

Disodium EDTA-based chelation therapy was associated with reducing a composite endpoint of mortality, recurrent MI, stroke, revascularization or hospitalization for angina when administered over 40 weekly infusions, driven largely by reduced revascularization procedures. This suggests further studies are needed into any possible beneficial effects from chelation in CAD.

Suxiao jiuxin wan appears to be slightly more effective than nitroglycerin and equally effective to isosorbide dinitrate in the treatment of angina pectoris resulting in reduced symptoms and frequency of attacks, with no reported serious side effects; study quality is poor.
Acupuncture has been shown to reduce angina over a short term relative to a sham procedure.
Cardiac rehabilitation programs, including exercise, are beneficial for exercise tolerance, risk factor management, and overall well being.
Psychosocial stress and depression management are believed to affect outcomes.
Increased adverse effects are associated with short-acting or immediate-release dihydropyridine calcium antagonists.
Meta-analysis of RCTs reveals that vitamin E is not useful for the primary or secondary prevention of heart disease and can be harmful at high doses (400 IU or more).
Ticlopidine does not have a CHD mortality/morbidity benefit and is associated with serious adverse effects, such as neutropenia and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
Dipyridamole potentiates exercise-induced ischemia and should not be used.
Sildenafil can be used in patients with SA unless contraindicated (e.g., in a patient taking a nitrate).
Lifestyle changes: lifelong.
Treatment with agents that provide a mortality/morbidity benefit: most likely lifelong.
Progressive angina.
Chest pain at rest.
Arrhythmias.
New onset CHF.
Potential complications include unstable angina and MI, arrhythmias and sudden death, and CHF.
See chapters on unstable angina, acute myocardial infarction, and heart failure.
Stress imaging (exercise/pharmacologic) is used to assess extent, severity, and location of ischemia. B
Resting LV function can be determined by echocardiography or radionuclide imaging and should be done for patients with prior MI or CHF symptoms/signs. B
Natural history of disease: asymptomatic, progressing to SA, progressive angina, angina at rest, acute MI, and finally death.

A subset of patients who have anginal symptoms may have angiographically normal coronaries or non-obstructive CAD. Such patients have a condition termed microvascular angina (MVA). They have coronary functional abnormalities due to epicardial coronary artery spasm and coronary microvascular dysfunction. The Coronary Vasomotor Disorders International Study group studied the clinical characteristics and health outcomes of patients with MVA in a large, prospective international registry and showed that patients with MVA are at substantial risk of MACE.
The prognosis depends on: (1) extent of LV dysfunction; (2) extent of atherosclerosis; (3) risk of coronary plaque rupture; and (4) general health and other comorbidities ().
Patients with major cardiac risk factors or those presenting at an earlier age tend to have more aggressive disease courses.
Focused history and physical every 4 to 12 months; depending on clinical status.
Address new concerns, symptoms, medication, and self-management challenges.
Labs: Diabetes screening every 3 years; fasting lipid profile 6 to 8 weeks after start of statin treatment and then periodically during the first year and then every 4 to 6 months.
ECG for new symptoms, findings, or medication changes.
Other tests as warranted for change in clinical status.
Notify your doctor if your symptoms worsen or change.
Ask your doctor for a healthy heart diet and exercise program.
Ask your doctor if you can take aspirin, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, or statins.
Know your blood pressure, cholesterol levels, blood sugar levels, and ideal weight range.
Stop smoking.
Diagnosis in elderly is complicated by the high frequency of chest pain and dyspnea complaints, higher frequency of abnormal ECG at rest, and functional limitations/inability to exercise.
Coronary angiography is associated with very little increased risk, although PCI tends to have a higher complication rate in patients over 80 years old.
Avoid teratogenic medications including ACE inhibitors and statins.

Assess for acute coronary syndrome or unstable angina.

Assess LV function.

Continue aspirin and beta-adrenergic blocking agent.

Initiate therapy to address lipid abnormalities.

Control hypertension.

Initiate tobacco use cessation.

Manage diabetes.

Manage depression.

Schedule regular follow-up.

feature.caption: Clinical Classification of Chest Pain.
feature.feature_body:
Typical Angina (definite)
(1) Substernal chest discomfort with a characteristic quality and duration that is (2) provoked by exertion or emotional stress and (3) relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Atypical Angina (probable)
Meets 2 of the above characteristics.
Noncardiac Chest Pain
Meets 1 or none of the above pain characteristics. Adapted from Diamond GA. A clinically relevant classification of chest discomfort. J Am Coll Cardiol 1983;1:574-575. Copyright © American College of Cardiology Foundation.

feature.caption: Grading of Angina Pectoris by the Canadian Cardiovascular Society Classification System.

list.listitem: Ordinary physical activity does not cause angina, such as walking, climbing stairs. Angina (occurs) with strenuous, rapid, or prolonged exertion at work or recreation.

Slight limitations of ordinary activity. Angina occurs on walking or climbing stairs rapidly, walking uphill, walking or stair climbing after meals, or in cold, in wind, or under emotional stress, or only during the few hours after awakening. Angina occurs on walking more than 2 blocks on the level and climbing more than one flight of ordinary stairs at a normal pace and in normal condition.
Marked limitations of ordinary physical activity. Angina occurs on walking 1 to 2 blocks on the level and climbing one flight of stairs in normal conditions and at a normal pace.

feature.caption: Prognosis.
feature.feature_body:
High Risk (greater than 3% annual mortality rate; 71%-79% 4-year survival)
Severe resting left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF <35%) High-risk treadmill score (score ≤-11) Severe exercise left ventricular dysfunction (exercise LVEF <35%) Stress-induced large perfusion defect (particularly if anterior) Stress-induced multiple perfusion defects of moderate size Large, fixed perfusion defect with LV dilation or increased lung uptake (thallium-201) Stress-induced moderate perfusion defect with LV dilation or increased lung uptake (thallium-201) Echocardiographic wall motion abnormality (involving more than 2 segments) developing at low dose of dobutamine (≤10 mg/kg/min) or at a low heart rate (<120 beats/min) Stress echocardiographic evidence of extensive ischemia
Intermediate Risk (1%-3% annual mortality rate; 92%-95% 4-year survival)
Mild/moderate resting left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF = 35%-49%) Intermediate-risk treadmill score (score ≥ −11 to <5) Stress-induced moderate perfusion defect without LV dilation or increased lung intake (thallium-201) Limited stress echocardiographic ischemia with a wall motion abnormality only at higher doses of dobutamine involving less than or equal to 2 segments
Low Risk (less than 1% annual mortality rate; 98%-99% 4-year survival)
Low-risk treadmill score (score ≥5) Normal or small myocardial perfusion defect at rest or with stress* Normal stress echocardiographic wall motion or no change of limited resting wall motion abnormalities during stress* *Although the published data are limited, patients with these findings will probably not be at low risk in the presence of either a high-risk treadmill score or severe resting left ventricular dysfunction (LVEF <35%). Adapted from Gibbons RJ, Balady GJ, Beasley JW, et al. ACC/AHA guidelines for exercise testing: executive summary.
